title: The Army takes over Tule Lake
pull: A camp under the Army's guns

facts.text: Tule Lake opened on 27 May 1942 near Newell in northern California, one of ten War Relocation Authority camps holding Japanese Americans forced from the West Coast.

In February 1943 the WRA gave a loyalty questionnaire to every incarcerated person aged 17 and older. Two questions asked if they would serve in combat wherever ordered and if they would swear unqualified allegiance to the United States and forswear any allegiance to the Japanese emperor.
On 15 July 1943 the WRA announced that anyone who answered no or refused to answer would be segregated. On 31 July Tule Lake was named the segregation center for people labeled 'disloyal.'
About 6,500 people were moved out to other camps and more than 12,000 were moved in. Tule Lake became the largest camp, holding about 18,700 people at its peak.
On 15 October 1943 a truck carrying farm workers overturned, killing one man. The farm workers went on strike over safety and conditions.

On 1 November 1943, during a visit by WRA director Dillon Myer, a crowd of 5,000 to 10,000 men, women and children gathered outside the administration building to back their elected Negotiating Committee, led by George Kuratomi.
On the evening of 4 November, people saw trucks leaving the warehouse area and believed camp food was going to strikebreakers. Scuffles broke out, and camp director Raymond Best called in the Army.
At 9:50 p.m. on 4 November, troops entered the camp and took over its administration. They came with tanks and jeeps mounted with machine guns.
Men seized that night were held in a tent stockade hastily put up in an open field. By December more than 200 men were held in the stockade, a prison inside the prison.
The Army declared martial law in mid November. It stayed in force until 15 January 1944.
An eight foot fence ringed the camp, and anyone leaving the barracks area needed a pass. The guard towers were manned first by the Army.
On 1 July 1944 President Roosevelt signed a law letting U.S. citizens renounce their citizenship in wartime. In all, 5,589 Japanese Americans renounced, most of them at Tule Lake.
Tule Lake was the last WRA camp to close, on 20 March 1946, seven months after the war ended.
